clue.text: Quiet, crafty person with a bias

parts.note: p is the musician's mark for piano, the direction to play quietly
a person who works at a craft is an artisan

explanation.surface: A hushed, sly operator who leans one way and makes no secret of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' is honest here, pointing at a craft worker rather than a schemer, and that sly second sense is the whole disguise. The comma after Quiet is the only join between the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan account leans one way before it begins, which is what saying it comes with a bias claims of it.

clue.text: Couple in power with attitude

parts.note: p is the physicist's letter for power
the manner someone gives off is an air, as in an air of grievance

explanation.surface: Two people whose influence comes with a certain manner about it.
explanation.walkthrough: An air is something worn rather than felt, which is why attitude covers it. P for power comes off the physics page, where it stands beside V for volts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair is two things taken and counted together, which is what a couple means of people or of anything else.

clue.text: Support check in respect of building material

parts.note: a rein checks a horse, and to rein something in is to check it
for and in respect of both mean as regards
the material named is cement

explanation.surface: A prop looked over as regards the stuff the builders will be using.
explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen letters arrive as three ordinary chunks with nothing to mark the joins, because a single long word invites nobody to look for them. 'For' standing in for 'in respect of' is the piece that hides best.
explanation.definitionFit: Reinforcement is whatever is added to make a thing hold — steel bars in concrete, fresh troops at the front — so it is support.

clue.text: Something that typifies popular motor race

parts.note: what is popular is in, as fashions are in or out
a motor is a car
race in the sense of a people, which is a nation

explanation.surface: A much-loved motor race that sums up everything its sport is about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motor race' reads as one event and is two words on separate errands, which is where the difficulty sits. Race for nation is the older sense of the word, a people rather than a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: An incarnation is a quality made flesh in one figure — the incarnation of patience — so it is something that typifies what it stands for.

clue.text: Plant from a covert US group covering California

indicators.note: What covers a thing lies over it on both sides, so the letters named next are shut inside the ones already made.

parts.note: the article taken as the letter it is written with
the Central Intelligence Agency is the United States' secret service, and the pair opens after the first letter
CA is California's two-letter postal code

explanation.surface: A shrub sent over by a secretive American agency whose reach extends across California.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as the spy the agency has placed and is the botanical definition. The wrapper is the article and the agency together, with the state dropped between them.
explanation.definitionFit: An acacia is a thorny tree or shrub of the pea family — the wattle of Australia, the flat-topped thorn of the African plains — so plant covers it.

clue.text: Fruit's sources of antioxidants can assist immunity

indicators.note: A source is where something starts, so each word named gives up the letter it starts with and nothing more.

parts.note: the opening letters of the four words, taken in the order they come

explanation.surface: A berry whose antioxidants are sold as a boost to the body's defences.
explanation.walkthrough: The health-food words read as a claim rather than a list, which is what keeps their initials out of sight. The apostrophe-s makes Fruit look possessive when it only marks where the definition stops.
explanation.definitionFit: The acai is the dark purple berry of a Brazilian palm, sold worldwide as pulp and juice, so it is a fruit.

clue.text: Terrible reactions over music school

indicators.note: terrible here means badly mangled, so the letters of the word are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the letters rearranged
the letters rearranged along with reactions

explanation.surface: Someone is going over a set of awful responses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a position word or a poetic O'ER, but here it simply joins REACTIONS as fodder: 'Terrible' scrambles all thirteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A conservatoire is a college for advanced training in music, the French-derived term for a conservatory.

clue.text: I would ultimately rate top-tier celebs as visionary

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I would

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of rate is used

parts.note: its last letter
the A-list is the top tier of celebrities

explanation.surface: Someone saying that, in the end, they would rank the most famous stars as people of vision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' takes the last letter of rate, which sits between I'D and A-LIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An idealist pursues high principles and a vision of how things should be, so is a visionary.

clue.text: Piece of memorabilia carved from bone

definitions.note: Iliac is an adjective, not the name of a bone: with 'from' in front of it the setter is asking for the word that means of that bone.

indicators.note: A piece of something is a part cut out of it, so a run of letters is lifted from the words that follow.

parts.note: the run bridging the two words: memorabILIA Carved

explanation.surface: A keepsake somebody cut and shaped out of bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bone' at the end looks like the material the keepsake is cut from, and it is the definition. The run straddles the space between two words, which is where a buried answer is hardest to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Iliac means belonging to the ilium, the broad flaring bone at the top of the hip, so the bare word bone points at it.

clue.text: Like trattoria food that's a bit hard to eat?

definitions.meaning: read as a grumble about the cooking in an Italian restaurant, and meant as the way that kitchen serves its pasta on purpose

definitions.text: that's a bit hard to eat?
definitions.meaning: read as food so tough that finishing it is a struggle, and meant as pasta boiled only until it still resists the tooth

explanation.surface: A complaint that the little Italian place serves dishes you can barely get through.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is Italian for 'to the tooth', so firmness is the point of it rather than a fault in the cooking. A trattoria is the cheaper, family-run sort of Italian restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta served al dente is cooked just short of soft, so it bites back a little, and the whole clue reads straight once hard means firm rather than inedible.

clue.text: Sensible BASE jumpers will go this way

definitions.meaning: level-headed and practical, with no airs about it

definitions.text: BASE jumpers will go this way
definitions.meaning: the direction anybody who steps off a tall structure travels, read as plainly as it is written

explanation.surface: Practical types who throw themselves off tall structures for the fun of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals in BASE are the tell: it is an acronym for what gets jumped off — building, antenna, span, earth. One half of the clue is a character judgement and the other is a direction of travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody down to earth is practical and free of airs, which is being sensible; a jumper's fall literally ends at the earth.

clue.text: Where rifles must be set out for fairground attraction

indicators.note: setting out the letters means laying them out afresh in a different order

parts.note: the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: At the funfair, the shooting gallery's guns need to be laid out somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The fairground setting suggests a rifle range stall, but 'must be set out' rearranges the letters of WHERE RIFLES.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ferris wheel is the giant upright rotating wheel with passenger cars found at funfairs and amusement parks.

clue.text: Very hot current circling river

indicators.note: Something circling goes round the outside of a thing, so the letters it names close around what follows.

parts.note: current in the sense of up to the minute is topical, and the word opens after its first letter
r = river, as it is shortened on maps

explanation.surface: A scalding flow of water turning circles in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' wants to belong to the river standing next to it, and it is the other sense entirely, up to the minute. The tropics are the belt either side of the equator, where the heat barely lets up.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical climate is the heavy unbroken heat of the equatorial belt, so tropical is a way of saying very hot.

clue.text: Take another look at doubly concerning publicity notice

indicators.note: Doubly means twice over, so the piece it points at goes down two times running.

parts.note: re is the letter-writer's word for concerning, and here it is written twice
ad is the everyday short form of advertisement

explanation.surface: A notice in the paper that gives cause for worry on two separate counts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' reads as troubling and is wanted as the office abbreviation meaning about, the one at the head of a memo. Doubling a piece is rare enough that the little word ordering it is easy to skate over.
explanation.definitionFit: To reread is to go through a text a second time, which is taking another look at it.

clue.text: Wooden slats in empty spice barrels put back

indicators.note: Something put back returns the way it came, so the letters named before it are read in the other direction.
A word emptied out has lost everything between its two ends, leaving only the letters at the front and the back.

parts.note: SPICE with its middle taken out keeps the S and the E
barrels for holding liquid are vats

explanation.surface: Emptied spice casks being turned round and put away again.
explanation.walkthrough: Slats, barrels and vats all belong to the cooper's yard, which is what holds the surface still while two instructions work underneath it. 'Empty' asking for the outside of a word is the step most often missed.
explanation.definitionFit: Staves are the shaped wooden strips that make up the sides of a barrel or a bucket, fitted edge to edge inside the hoops.

clue.text: Picture snapper arrived with artist

parts.note: arrived in the past tense is came
RA is a Royal Academician, the letters a British artist elected to the Royal Academy puts after their name

explanation.surface: A press photographer who turned up in the company of a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Snapper reads as the person behind the lens, and the agent noun sits as well on the machine doing the snapping. Camera is Latin for a vaulted chamber, after the dark room light was first let into.
explanation.definitionFit: A camera is the thing that takes the picture, so 'picture snapper' names the box by the job it does rather than by what it is.

clue.text: American guys inside foresee trouble

indicators.note: What is inside a thing sits within its walls, so the letters named before go within the word that follows.

parts.note: to foresee something is to predict it, and the word opens before its last letter
a = American, the A of USA
guys are men

explanation.surface: Americans in the building can see difficulty coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' reads as being indoors long before it reads as an instruction, and the two short pieces slip in without the sentence stumbling. Predict parting at its final T is what leaves room for them.
explanation.definitionFit: A predicament is a tight spot with no easy way out of it, which is what trouble means when you are in it.

clue.text: Individual taking Charlie a single time

indicators.note: A word taking something receives it within itself, so the letter named next is set inside the one before.

parts.note: an individual is one, and the word parts after the first two letters
Charlie is the radio alphabet's word for C

explanation.surface: A lone figure accepting cocaine, just the one time.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is street slang for cocaine, which is what the surface is selling, and the signaller's codeword for C, which is what the clue needs. Only the letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Once means on one occasion and no more, which is what doing something a single time amounts to.

clue.text: Remove contaminants from various lances before start of examination

indicators.note: before places the jumbled letters ahead of the letter from examination
various means of different kinds, so the letters of lances are put into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: Sterilising a set of surgical lances before a medical examination begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Various' rearranges LANCES into CLEANS, and 'start of' adds the E of examination.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleanse is to make thoroughly clean, which is to rid something of contaminants.

clue.text: Come down to the audience and hold sway

indicators.note: An audience takes a word in by ear, so what is wanted is how it sounds rather than how it is spelt.

parts.note: what comes down out of the sky is rain, and the two spellings are said exactly alike

explanation.surface: A performer stepping off the stage to the crowd and taking charge of the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come down to the audience' reads as a speaker leaving the platform, and that is where the sound is buried. Rain, reign and rein are three spellings of one noise, so only the definition picks between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To reign is to rule as monarch, and by extension to be the force holding sway over everything around.

clue.text: Instrument featuring regularly in Alouette

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval, every other one and none of those between.

parts.note: every second letter of aLoUeTtE

explanation.surface: An instrument that keeps cropping up in a well-known song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Featuring regularly' reads as an instrument often heard in the piece, which is the cover for picking letters at intervals. Alouette is the French-Canadian round about plucking a lark, italicised here because it is a title.
explanation.definitionFit: The lute is the pear-bodied plucked string instrument of Renaissance Europe, the ancestor of the guitar.

clue.text: Payment option being nothing more than fine fabric

parts.note: one of the ways offered to pay is cash
a mere something is nothing more than that

explanation.surface: Settling the bill with nothing better to hand than a length of good cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing more than' is doing the work of one adjective, mere, and reads as a dismissal instead. Cashmere is named for Kashmir, where the goats whose undercoat it comes from are bred.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is the soft fine wool combed from the undercoat of Kashmir goats and woven into cloth, so it is a fine fabric.
